hero.headline: US launches strikes on Iran after helicopter downing
hero.body:
The United States military launched retaliatory strikes against Iran on Tuesday evening following Iran's downing of an American Apache helicopter near the Strait of Hormuz. US Central Command forces began the strikes at 5 p.m. Eastern Time at President Trump's direction, describing them as a proportional response.

The Apache helicopter crashed off the coast of Oman early Tuesday morning while on patrol. Both crew members were rescued in an unprecedented operation using an unmanned drone boat called a Corsair, a 24-foot vessel. The military confirmed both aviators were safe and uninjured after spending roughly two hours in the water.

President Trump announced the incident on Truth Social, stating that Iran had shot down the helicopter. "There were two pilots involved, both are safe and uninjured. Nevertheless, the United States must, of necessity, respond to the attack," Trump wrote. The actual cause of the crash remained under investigation, though Trump attributed it to Iranian action.

The retaliatory strikes came as tensions escalated in the Middle East following recent exchanges between Iran and Israel. Iranian state television reported that Israeli attacks killed at least two members of the country's air defense units. The region has remained unstable since the US and Israel began striking Iran on February 28, which has disrupted global energy prices and raised the cost of food and other essentials worldwide.

Apache helicopters have been critical assets for American military operations in the region, particularly for enforcing a blockade on Iranian crude oil shipments designed to pressure Tehran into making a deal. The helicopters have also been used by the United Arab Emirates to shoot down Iranian drones.

Despite the military action, Trump indicated he remains optimistic about negotiations with Iran. Earlier Tuesday, before the helicopter incident, Trump expressed confidence that a deal could be reached within "two or three days," though he provided no details supporting this assessment.

Trump previously stated that while the US could conduct extensive bombing campaigns, doing so would be costly in both lives and time. "If we go and bomb, which we could do very easily if we want, and we spend another two or three weeks bombing, they'll have nothing left whatsoever. But you won't have the strait open for months," he said. "If we do the bombing, you know, a lot of people are going to be killed. Who wants to do that? I don't."

Iranian state media reported explosions in Hormozgan province, which borders the Strait of Hormuz, following the announcement of US strikes. Central Command has not disclosed the specific targets of the military action.

The situation highlights the delicate balance the Trump administration is attempting to maintain: responding forcefully enough to the loss of military assets while preserving space for continued diplomatic negotiations with Iran.

cards.headline: House passes $70 billion bill to fund immigration enforcement through end of Trump term
cards.body:
The House of Representatives passed legislation providing $70 billion in funding for immigration enforcement agencies over the next three years, ensuring that the Department of Homeland Security, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and Customs and Border Protection remain funded through September 2029.

The bill, known as the Secure America Act, allocates $38 billion to ICE, $26 billion to Customs and Border Protection, and $5 billion to the Department of Homeland Security. House Republicans advanced the measure on Tuesday by a narrow margin, with the final vote coming down to a single lawmaker's decision.

Republican Tim Walberg of Michigan initially voted against the legislation, which would have resulted in a 213-213 tie and killed the measure. After being surrounded by House Republican leaders, Walberg changed his vote, allowing the bill to pass. The measure now heads to President Trump's desk for his signature.

The Senate had already passed the bill the previous week. In the House, debate over the measure advanced on a party-line vote of 213-211, reflecting the slim Republican majority. One Republican member, Tom Kean Jr., has been absent for months due to a health crisis, further narrowing the margin for passage.

Republicans have characterized the funding as essential support for Trump's immigration enforcement agenda. The extended funding period eliminates the need for annual congressional reauthorization of these agencies, giving immigration enforcement operations sustained resources without requiring regular legislative review.

Democrats have criticized the approach, arguing that Congress has surrendered a crucial oversight mechanism. By approving long-term funding without built-in review mechanisms, lawmakers have removed a traditional tool used to maintain accountability over executive branch agencies and their operations.

The bill sparked particular concern among Democrats regarding provisions related to compensation for January 6 rioters. Representative Bennie Thompson, the Mississippi Democrat who chaired the 2022 select committee investigation of the Capitol attack, noted that the bill does not include a provision that would have prevented the Department of Justice from paying Trump supporters convicted of attacking police officers during the riot up to $1.776 billion.

The legislation focuses exclusively on enforcement operations and does not include funding for immigration courts, legal services, or other components of the immigration system. Immigration advocacy groups have expressed concern about the scale of enforcement funding without corresponding investment in due process infrastructure.

The passage comes after weeks of debate among Republican lawmakers about the bill's scope and structure. The measure represents one of the largest single appropriations for immigration enforcement in recent history, cementing Trump's immigration priorities into law through multiple years of guaranteed funding.

cards.headline: Social Security trust fund projected to run out in 2032, threatening benefit cuts
cards.body:
The Social Security retirement trust fund will be depleted by late 2032 unless Congress takes action, according to new projections that moved the insolvency date forward by several years. The program, which supports roughly 68 million Americans, faces an accelerated shortfall that could result in automatic benefit cuts averaging 22 percent for all recipients.

The updated timeline represents a significant shift from previous estimates and reflects changing economic conditions and demographic trends. Social Security relies on payroll taxes to fund monthly benefits for retirees, disabled workers, and survivors of deceased workers. When the trust fund runs dry, the program will only be able to pay out what it collects in current taxes, forcing across-the-board reductions unless lawmakers intervene.

The 2032 deadline puts pressure on Congress to address the funding gap through some combination of tax increases, benefit adjustments, or other reforms. Options under consideration have included raising the retirement age, increasing the payroll tax cap, or adjusting cost-of-living calculations. Each approach faces political resistance, and previous attempts at reform have stalled despite bipartisan acknowledgment of the problem.

The accelerated timeline reflects broader concerns about the program's long-term sustainability as the baby boomer generation continues to retire and draw benefits. The worker-to-beneficiary ratio has declined as the population ages, putting additional strain on the system. Economic factors, including wage growth patterns and labor force participation rates, also influence the trust fund's trajectory.

The announcement underscores the urgency of legislative action to preserve benefits for current and future retirees. Financial planners have begun advising clients to consider the possibility of reduced benefits when making retirement plans. Advocacy groups representing seniors have called on Congress to prioritize a solution before the 2032 deadline, warning that waiting until the last moment could result in more drastic cuts or tax increases than would be necessary with earlier intervention.

cards.headline: Trump faces pressure to drop intelligence nominee over spy powers renewal
cards.teaser: Democrats threaten to block FISA renewal unless the president withdraws Bill Pulte's nomination.
cards.body:
President Trump is set to meet with House Speaker Mike Johnson at the White House as pressure mounts to nominate a permanent director of national intelligence. The move comes as Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act faces a deadline for renewal by the end of the week.

Section 702 allows US intelligence agencies to collect communications of foreign targets overseas without a court warrant, though the surveillance can also capture communications involving Americans. Some Republicans believe appointing a permanent intelligence chief is necessary to save the controversial surveillance program before it expires.

cards.headline: Israeli Strikes Hit Lebanese City of Tyre Amid Evacuation Warnings
cards.teaser: Israeli forces struck the ancient Lebanese city of Tyre as Christian leaders called for international intervention.
cards.body:
Israeli air strikes targeted the Lebanese city of Tyre as Iran warned Israel that it could resume hostilities if attacks on Hezbollah continue. Israeli authorities ordered residents to evacuate ahead of the operations in southern Lebanon.

Christian leaders in Tyre called for swift international intervention following the Israeli evacuation warning. The ancient coastal city faced bombardment despite not being a major target in previous Israeli military operations against Hezbollah in the region.

cards.headline: Earthquake in Philippines Traps Many Under Rubble
cards.teaser: Rescue efforts continue after the most powerful earthquake to strike the Philippines in 50 years.
cards.body:
A magnitude-7.8 earthquake struck off the coast of Sarangani province in southern Philippines early Monday, killing at least 37 people and injuring hundreds. The powerful quake collapsed buildings across the region and was felt strongly throughout Mindanao and as far away as Manado in Indonesia.

Emergency responders urged people to avoid damaged buildings due to the risk of aftershocks. Rescue operations continued as families searched for loved ones trapped beneath the debris.

cards.headline: Myanmar Rebels Lose Ground as Military Forces Conscription
cards.teaser: Rebel forces in Myanmar face setbacks as the military junta expands conscription efforts.
cards.body:
Rebel groups in Myanmar are losing territory as the military government intensifies forced conscription efforts to bolster its ranks. The junta has expanded control over areas previously held by opposition forces, marking a significant shift in the conflict that erupted after the 2021 military coup.

Journalists embedded with rebel forces have documented the deteriorating situation at frontline positions across the country. The military's aggressive recruitment campaign reflects its strategy to reverse earlier territorial losses and reassert dominance over opposition-held regions.

cards.headline: UK and Allies Impose Sanctions on Networks Supporting West Bank Settler Violence
cards.teaser: Britain joined international partners in sanctioning individuals and networks enabling attacks by Israeli settlers.
cards.body:
The United Kingdom and allied nations have imposed sanctions targeting networks that enable settler violence against Palestinians in the West Bank. France announced it will bar Israeli Minister Bezalel Smotrich from entering the country as part of these coordinated measures. Israel has condemned the sanctions as "disgraceful."

The sanctions focus on financial and logistical networks supporting violent actions by Israeli settlers in occupied Palestinian territories. This diplomatic action represents an effort by European governments to address escalating violence in the West Bank through economic penalties.

cards.headline: Hundreds Protest Immigration in Belfast After Stabbing Attack
cards.teaser: Demonstrations erupted across Northern Ireland following a knife attack that was recorded and shared online.
cards.body:
Hundreds of people rallied against immigration in Belfast following a stabbing incident. Police arrested a 30-year-old Sudanese man and charged him in connection with the attack, which was recorded and widely shared on social media.

The demonstrations spread beyond Belfast to other parts of Scotland as tensions over immigration policy intensified. Protesters set vehicles on fire during the unrest, prompting UK leaders to call for calm.

cards.headline: AI Company Releases Tool Previously Deemed Too Powerful for Public Use
cards.teaser: Anthropic made public a version of Claude Mythos that had caused concern among technology and government leaders.
cards.body:
A version of an artificial intelligence tool that developers had deemed too powerful for public release has been made available. Claude Fable 5 is a version of Anthropic's Claude Mythos, an AI program that previously caused concern among leaders in technology, finance, and government sectors.

The decision to release the tool represents a reversal from earlier caution about making the advanced AI system publicly accessible. Anthropic had not disclosed what specific capabilities prompted the initial determination that the technology should be restricted.

cards.headline: Former Air Canada Pilot Accused of Flying Without Proper License for 17 Years
cards.teaser: Police say a pilot flew hundreds of commercial flights over nearly two decades without the necessary qualifications.
cards.body:
Geoffrey Wall of Barrie, Ontario, has been charged after operating as an Air Canada captain between 2009 and 2025 without a license to fly large commercial passenger planes, according to Peel regional police. Wall allegedly flew over 900 flights on both domestic and international routes during this period.

The case raises significant questions about Air Canada's credentialing and oversight procedures, as the pilot's alleged lack of proper qualifications went undetected for more than a decade and a half while carrying thousands of passengers.

cards.headline: US launches strikes against Iran after helicopter downing
cards.teaser: The military confirmed strikes on Iran following the downing of a US helicopter over the Strait of Hormuz.
cards.body:
United States Central Command confirmed that American forces struck targets in Iran following the downing of a US Apache helicopter near the Strait of Hormuz. President Trump blamed Iran for the attack and stated that a US response was necessary.

The Apache helicopter crashed off the coast of Oman early Tuesday morning. Both crew members were safely rescued in an operation using an unmanned drone boat, marking an unprecedented recovery effort. The incident represents a significant escalation in tensions between the two nations in the strategic waterway.

cards.headline: World Cup visitors face heightened immigration screening at US entry points
cards.teaser: Match officials and team members have encountered enhanced scrutiny when attempting to enter the United States ahead of the tournament.
cards.body:
As the World Cup begins this week, foreign nationals involved in the tournament are encountering stricter immigration screening at U.S. entry points. A FIFA referee from Somalia was denied entry under these enhanced procedures. Match officials and team members from various countries have experienced delays and additional questioning while attempting to enter the United States.

The heightened vetting has created uncertainty for international participants. The stricter immigration policies appear designed to increase security measures during the global event, though they have created challenges for those seeking to attend or participate in World Cup activities.

cards.headline: White House restricts press access during UFC event
cards.teaser: Reporters will be barred from the White House during a UFC fight unless the sports organization provides credentials.
cards.body:
The White House will close its facilities to reporters during an upcoming UFC fight unless the sports organization grants press credentials. This shifts control of journalist access from the White House press office to the private UFC organization.

The event has prompted extensive road closures throughout Washington. A Trump-backed super PAC is organizing a fundraiser the day before the fight, with tickets priced at $1 million per person.

cards.headline: South Carolina holds midterm primary elections
cards.teaser: Voters cast ballots in statewide primaries with polls closing at 7 p.m.
cards.body:
South Carolina conducted primary elections with races including the Republican contest to select a nominee to replace Governor McMaster. Polling locations remained open until 7 p.m. across the state.

Results began arriving as polls closed, with voters selecting candidates for various statewide offices. The primaries determine which candidates will advance to the general election ballot.

cards.headline: Teen convicted of murder in fatal stabbing at Texas high school track meet
cards.teaser: Karmelo Anthony was found guilty of murder in the death of Frisco student Austin Metcalf.
cards.body:
A jury in Texas convicted Karmelo Anthony, 19, of murder for fatally stabbing Austin Metcalf during a high school track meet in Frisco in April 2025. The one-week trial drew national attention, partly due to the racial composition of the case: Anthony is Black and Metcalf was white. None of the 12 jurors selected was Black.

The stabbing occurred when a rain shower caused confusion at the track meet. While some athletes sought shelter, others remained on the field. When Anthony, from Centennial High School, sought cover under Memorial High School's tent, a confrontation erupted. Metcalf, also 17 at the time, was fatally wounded and pronounced dead shortly after arriving at the hospital.

cards.headline: West Ham director banned from contact with women's and youth teams
cards.teaser: David Sullivan has been prohibited from interacting with certain West Ham teams since 2023 following a safeguarding investigation.
cards.body:
The Football Association opened a safeguarding investigation that resulted in David Sullivan being banned from contact with West Ham's women's and youth teams. The restriction has been in place since 2023.

Sullivan, who serves as co-chair of West Ham United, stepped down from his position ahead of allegations concerning his private life, which he has denied.

cards.headline: SpaceX IPO attracts nearly four times more demand than shares available
cards.teaser: Orders for SpaceX stock have reached roughly $250 billion as the company prepares for its highly anticipated public offering with a price already set.
cards.body:
SpaceX is preparing for what's being called the biggest stock market launch in history. The company plans to release 555.6 million shares on June 12 at a $135 valuation, raising $75 billion from the sale. Demand for the offering is approaching four times oversubscription, far exceeding available shares.

Up to a quarter of the shares could be reserved for individual investors rather than institutional funds and banks—a notably larger retail allocation than typical for major IPOs.

cards.headline: General Motors to manufacture large-scale energy storage batteries
cards.teaser: The automaker will produce batteries for electric utilities and data centers as electric vehicle sales growth slows.
cards.body:
General Motors announced plans to manufacture large-scale energy storage batteries for electric utilities, data centers, and other businesses. The move follows Tesla's successful entry into the stationary battery market and represents GM's effort to diversify beyond automotive applications as EV sales growth slows.

GM is developing a new sodium-ion battery chemistry for energy storage applications. The company also announced vehicle-to-grid capabilities for its current EV and home energy customers, positioning electric vehicles as tools to help manage the electrical grid's growing power demands, particularly from AI data centers.

cards.headline: Stock indexes fall as technology shares resume decline
cards.teaser: The S&P 500 and Nasdaq closed lower while oil prices dropped to a seven-week low after Iran and Israel agreed to halt strikes.
cards.body:
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq declined Tuesday as technology stocks came under renewed pressure, with semiconductor shares unable to maintain earlier gains. The Dow Jones Industrial Average bucked the trend to finish higher.

Oil prices fell below $90 per barrel, marking their lowest point in seven weeks, after Israel and Iran agreed to cease retaliatory strikes. The de-escalation of Middle East tensions eased concerns about potential regional conflict that had previously supported crude prices.

cards.headline: FDA approves new sunscreen ingredient after decades-long wait
cards.teaser: Regulators cleared a UV-blocking compound that has been used in Europe and Asia for years, marking the first new sunscreen ingredient in almost 30 years.
cards.body:
The Food and Drug Administration approved a new sunscreen ingredient that has been available in European and Asian markets for years, ending a regulatory drought that stretched more than 25 years. The approval marks the first addition to the list of permitted sunscreen active ingredients in the United States since the late 1990s.

The newly approved compound provides protection against ultraviolet radiation and brings American sunscreen formulations closer to options already available to consumers in other developed countries. The lengthy approval process reflects the FDA's rigorous safety and efficacy standards for over-the-counter drug ingredients.

cards.headline: California considers legal challenge to Paramount-Warner Bros. merger
cards.teaser: The state is in talks with a prominent technology lawyer to examine the $110 billion media deal that has drawn scrutiny from regulators.
cards.body:
California officials are consulting with a prominent technology attorney about potentially challenging the Paramount Skydance merger with Warner Bros. Discovery, sources say. The $110 billion deal has drawn scrutiny from regulators over concerns about market concentration in entertainment.

The UK's Competition and Markets Authority has launched a formal investigation into the transaction. The merged company would control major streaming platforms including Paramount and HBO Max, as well as sports broadcasting rights for the Champions League, Premier League and Olympics, plus major film and television studios.

cards.headline: Penn Station set for $8 billion renovation under new plan
cards.teaser: New York's busiest train station will undergo a major remodel featuring classical columns and natural light, with the project to bear President Trump's name.
cards.body:
New York's Pennsylvania Station will undergo an $8 billion renovation to address long-standing complaints about the transit hub. The redesign will add classical architectural columns and increase natural light throughout the facility, which currently features cramped underground concourses.

The project is part of a redevelopment agreement that will carry President Trump's name. Penn Station serves hundreds of thousands of commuters daily and has faced decades of calls for improvements to modernize one of the nation's most heavily used transportation facilities.

hero.headline: NASA names crew for Artemis III moon mission
hero.body:
NASA announced the four-person crew selected for its Artemis III mission, representing the next phase in the agency's effort to return astronauts to the lunar surface. The crew will launch in 2027 for a two-week mission to low Earth orbit designed to test critical systems before planned lunar landings.

The selected crew includes NASA astronaut and commander Randy Bresnik, European Space Agency pilot Luca Parmitano, and NASA mission specialists Frank Rubio and Andre Douglas. Parmitano, an Italian astronaut, will serve as pilot for the mission. One crew member is a University of Michigan alumnus.

It is important to note that the Artemis III crew will not land on the moon or travel to the lunar surface. Instead, they will remain in Earth orbit while testing lunar landers developed by private companies SpaceX and Blue Origin. This mission serves as a preparatory step for future moon landings rather than the landing mission itself.

NASA administrator Jared Isaacman described the crew selection as part of creating "Earth's first starfleet" and emphasized the significance of the next stages in NASA's moon return program. The Artemis III mission represents a continuation of the broader Artemis program, which began with the uncrewed Artemis I test flight and continued with the crewed Artemis II lunar flyby that recently completed a record-breaking journey around the moon.

The space agency has positioned Artemis as its pathway back to the lunar surface after a gap of more than 50 years since the final Apollo mission. NASA aims to land astronauts on the moon through the Artemis IV mission planned for 2028. When humans do return to the lunar surface, the missions will mark a historic milestone by including the first woman and first person of color to walk on the moon.

The Artemis program faces ongoing scrutiny regarding its ambitious timeline. Technical challenges and development delays have affected various components of the program, and questions persist about whether NASA can meet its target dates. Some reports suggest that crew members may face disappointment if the program experiences further delays that prevent them from achieving their mission objectives.

Beyond lunar exploration, NASA has positioned the Artemis program as a stepping stone toward eventual human missions to Mars. The program represents a significant expansion of human spaceflight ambitions and international collaboration, with participation from the European Space Agency alongside American space agencies and private companies.

The crew selection drew from NASA's experienced astronaut corps, with considerations given to training, experience, and specific mission requirements. The announcement reflects NASA's commitment to advancing human space exploration in the coming years.

cards.headline: Google launches Gemini 3.5 Live Translate for voice-to-voice translation
cards.teaser: The new feature preserves speaker tone and pacing while providing instant translation between languages.
cards.body:
Google has announced Gemini 3.5 Live Translate, enabling instant voice-to-voice translation that preserves a speaker's tone, pacing, and pitch. The system moves beyond robotic or text-based translations by maintaining the emotional and contextual qualities of the original speech.

The technology incorporates SynthID watermarks to authenticate and track AI-generated audio. This security feature allows Google to verify the origin of translated voice content while enabling more natural conversations across language barriers.

cards.headline: GM developing sodium-ion batteries for data centers and grid storage
cards.teaser: General Motors is creating a new battery chemistry aimed at powering AI infrastructure and industrial facilities.
cards.body:
General Motors is developing sodium-ion battery technology for use in data centers and its own manufacturing facilities. The new battery chemistry represents an alternative to the lithium-ion systems traditionally used in electric vehicles.

GM's move into battery production for data centers reflects the surging power demands of AI computing infrastructure. The company is positioning itself in the growing market for energy storage solutions beyond conventional lithium-based systems.

cards.headline: Anthropic's Claude Fable 5 generates video games from text prompts
cards.teaser: The AI model can create playable games based on simple text instructions.
cards.body:
Anthropic announced Claude Fable 5, its first publicly available model from the Mythos class. The company describes it as the most powerful model it has made widely available, demonstrating exceptional performance in software engineering, knowledge work, and vision tasks. The model's advantages over competitors increase with longer and more complex tasks.

The release includes built-in safeguards that prevent the model from responding to queries in high-risk areas including cybersecurity, biology, and chemistry. Among its capabilities, Fable 5 can generate video games from text prompts, enabling users without traditional programming skills to create interactive experiences.

cards.headline: Apple introduces subscription bundles for App Store developers
cards.teaser: Developers will gain new tools to package multiple subscriptions together for users.
cards.body:
Apple is expanding its App Store bundles feature to let developers create discounted subscription packages together. The new offering works similarly to streaming video bundles—like combined Apple TV and Peacock deals—but applies to app subscriptions across different companies and services.

The move is part of Apple's broader effort to give developers more tools to market and sell their products. The company is also introducing personalized app recommendations to help users discover new applications, alongside expanded capabilities designed to help developers reach wider audiences on the platform.

cards.headline: Anthropic restricts Claude Fable 5 from answering questions on cybersecurity and biology
cards.teaser: The company implemented topic blocks on its frontier AI model for safety reasons.
cards.body:
Anthropic has released Claude Fable 5, its first Mythos-class model available to the general public. The company implemented guardrails that prevent the model from responding to queries in high-risk areas including cybersecurity, biology, and chemistry.

According to Anthropic, Claude Fable 5 demonstrates exceptional performance in software engineering, knowledge work, and vision tasks, with its advantages over competing models becoming more pronounced on longer and more complex assignments. The restrictions reflect the company's approach to managing potential risks associated with powerful AI systems.

cards.headline: Apple adjusts Liquid Glass interface controls in macOS Golden Gate
cards.teaser: Users gain more control over the controversial visual design element introduced in recent operating system updates.
cards.body:
Apple made changes to Liquid Glass controls in macOS Golden Gate, allowing users to adjust the intensity of the interface effect. The company added a slider that can be pushed to ultra settings, giving users greater customization over the visual appearance of the operating system.

The adjustments follow user feedback about the Liquid Glass design element, which Apple introduced in earlier software versions. Apple also extended similar controls to iOS 27, letting users dial down the effect across its operating systems. The changes indicate Apple's response to varied user preferences about the interface design.

hero.headline: Serena Williams wins doubles match in return to tennis after nearly four years
hero.body:
Serena Williams made a successful competitive return to professional tennis at age 44, winning her first match in 1,375 days. Playing alongside Canadian teenager Victoria Mboko, Williams defeated third seeds Nicole Melichar-Martinez and Erin Routliffe 7-6 (7-2), 6-2 in the opening round of doubles at Queen's Club in London.

Williams last competed professionally in September 2022 when she stepped away from tennis following the US Open. The 23-time Grand Slam singles champion has described her return as focused on enjoyment rather than achievement. "I don't need to win. I've won more than most people have in their whole lives," Williams said. "For me it's not important. I don't have anything to prove, I don't have anything to lose and everything here is just a gain."

The match itself proved competitive, particularly in the opening set. With the score balanced at 5-5, 30-30, Williams fired down a 120mph service winner to help secure the hold. The unseeded pair controlled the tiebreak, winning 7-2, then dominated the second set to close out the match decisively.

Williams selected Mboko as her partner after being impressed by the world number 9 in singles. "She reminded me a lot of myself," Williams explained. "I remember seeing her play in Montreal. I was impressed with her attitude, and what I liked the most about her was that the next time she played she still kept winning."

For Mboko, who was only 10 years old when Williams won her last Grand Slam title, the partnership held special significance. "Growing up, Serena has always been my idol," said the Canadian. "Seeing someone on TV versus actually talking to them in person and having conversations, of course, it's very different. I think she's really nice and very personable, very relatable."

Williams has committed to competing in doubles in Berlin following the Queen's tournament, though her plans beyond that remain uncertain. When asked about returning to singles competition, she said: "I can't say yeah, I can't say no. Right now, no." She added that she would likely need additional training if she decides to play singles events.

The 44-year-old emphasized that her primary motivation for competing is personal rather than professional. "It's really about my kids getting to see me play," she said, referencing her daughters Olympia, aged eight, and two-year-old Adira. "It's summer, the kids aren't in school, so it's a perfect time to get out there, have fun and see what happens."

Williams and Mboko will advance to the second round of the grass-court event, which serves as key preparation for Wimbledon later this month.

cards.headline: Real Madrid's $150 million bid for Julian Alvarez rejected by Atletico
cards.teaser: Atletico Madrid turned down a substantial offer from their city rivals for the striker.
cards.body:
Real Madrid's €150 million bid for striker Julian Alvarez has been rejected by Atletico Madrid. The Argentina international, who joined Atletico from Manchester City in 2024, has scored 49 goals in 106 appearances for the club.

The 26-year-old's contract runs until 2030, though he reportedly wants to leave. Real Madrid president Florentino Pérez had previously pledged to make a club-record offer for a top player following his reelection.

cards.headline: Emma Raducanu wins opening match in Wimbledon preparations at Queen's
cards.teaser: The British player began her grass-court season with a straight-set victory.
cards.body:
Emma Raducanu made a dominant start to her grass-court season, defeating Russia's Anna Blinkova 6-0 6-3 in her opening match at Queen's Club. The British number one advanced to the second round with a commanding performance.

Raducanu expressed her satisfaction with the win, describing it as a strong stepping stone for the month ahead. She highlighted her enjoyment of how she moved and performed on court, stating she wants to carry that confidence into her remaining matches as she prepares for Wimbledon.

cards.headline: SoFi Stadium workers reach labor agreement, averting World Cup strike
cards.teaser: The tentative deal comes days before the Los Angeles venue hosts World Cup matches.
cards.body:
Workers at SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles reached a tentative labor agreement on Tuesday, averting a strike that could have disrupted World Cup matches. The deal covers cashiers, dishwashers, cooks, bartenders, concessions workers and food attendants at the venue.

The timing was critical, with the US's opening match against Paraguay scheduled for June 12 at the stadium. The union retained contractual rights to strike if federal immigration enforcement threatens worker safety during the tournament.

cards.headline: Iran says World Cup ticket allocation withdrawn days before tournament
cards.teaser: The Iranian football federation reported that tickets designated for fans were revoked.
cards.body:
Iran's football federation said the ticket allocation for Iranian fans attending World Cup matches was withdrawn days before the tournament begins. The federation announced the revocation of tickets that had been designated for supporters.

The US Department of Homeland Security separately stated that Iranian World Cup players will be permitted to enter the United States the day before their matches. Iranian players arrived in Mexico ahead of the tournament, wearing pins honoring victims of a deadly strike on a school.

cards.headline: England managing Bukayo Saka's fitness ahead of World Cup
cards.teaser: Head coach Thomas Tuchel said the Arsenal winger is receiving careful treatment.
cards.body:
England head coach Thomas Tuchel is managing Bukayo Saka's fitness carefully as the World Cup draws near. The Arsenal winger is receiving particular attention from the coaching staff regarding his physical condition ahead of the tournament.

Saka, 24, is a key attacking player for England and will play an important role in the team's World Cup campaign. Tuchel's comments suggest the team is taking a cautious approach with the winger's preparation.

cards.headline: Knicks fans arrested after Game 3 loss in NBA Finals
cards.teaser: Police made 21 arrests following disorderly behavior after a watch party in Bryant Park.
cards.body:
New York police arrested 21 people and five NYPD officers were injured following disorderly behavior after the Knicks lost Game 3 of the NBA Finals to the San Antonio Spurs. The incidents occurred in Midtown Manhattan as crowds dispersed from a watch party in Bryant Park.

Videos circulating on social media documented apparent attacks on Spurs fans, including incidents where jerseys were ripped off. Players from both teams condemned the violence, with San Antonio's Victor Wembanyama among those calling the attacks unacceptable.

hero.headline: Guitarist James Blood Ulmer Dies at 86
hero.body:
James Blood Ulmer, the innovative guitarist who merged avant-garde jazz with blues and funk into a distinctive sound, has died at 86. He died on June 3, according to a statement from his family, who described him as fearless in both music and spirit.

Born Willie James Ulmer in South Carolina in 1940, he began his music career playing in funk bands across Pittsburgh, Columbus, and Detroit, backing musicians including Jewel Bryner and Hank Marr. After settling in New York in the early 1970s, Ulmer fundamentally changed his approach to music. "I ain't never thought nobody could make no money playing free music," he later reflected. "So I always played structured blues, rhythm playing, dance music, or something like that. And I abandoned it! When I came to New York, it was like I just went totally another way."

In New York, Ulmer performed with Art Blakey, Joe Henderson, and Rashied Ali while studying under avant-garde pioneer Ornette Coleman. Coleman taught him his harmolodic theory, which rejected traditional keys and harmonics in favor of a freer approach to sound. This philosophy would shape Ulmer's entire career, influencing his instinctive, unbounded playing style even as he began writing songs.

Coleman co-produced Ulmer's debut album "Tales of Captain Black." His next release, "Are You Glad to Be in America?" on the British Rough Trade label, featured a spirited social commentary title track that became his signature song. Ulmer went on to support punk and rock bands including Public Image Ltd and Captain Beefheart, bringing an aggressive energy to these collaborations. When addressing crowds at these performances, he was direct: "I'd stand at the microphone and tell them to shut the fuck up. They had five minutes to get into it or get the fuck out!"

Collaborations with saxophonist Arthur Blythe on albums like "Lenox Avenue Breakdown" and "Illusions" led to Ulmer securing a record deal with Columbia. Between 1981 and 1983, he released three progressive albums: "Free Lancing," "Black Rock," and "Odyssey." Rolling Stone hailed him in "Free Lancing" as "the most original electric guitarist to emerge since the late Jimi Hendrix." These records paired virtuosic bluesy guitar work with tight funk arrangements and soulful vocals.

Ulmer also formed the Music Revelation Ensemble with saxophonist David Murray, bassist Amin Ali, and drummer Ronald Shannon Jackson, debuting with "No Wave" in 1980. He later founded another group, Phalanx, reconnecting with Ali.

Following his Columbia years, Ulmer continued recording prolifically through subsequent decades, gradually focusing more on blues than jazz. His 2001 album "Memphis Blood: The Sun Sessions" earned his only Grammy nomination, for best traditional blues album. He also appeared on recordings by Ry Cooder and hip-hop group the Roots, among others. Ulmer retired in 2024 after performing his final concert at Detroit's jazz festival.

cards.headline: Chris Brown Settles Lawsuit Over Song Credits
cards.teaser: The singer resolved a legal dispute with a lyricist over credit and revenue for songs Monalisa and Sensational.
cards.body:
Chris Brown has settled a lawsuit filed by a lyricist who accused him of denying proper credit and excluding the plaintiff from millions in revenue. The dispute centered on two songs, Monalisa and Sensational.

The lawsuit claimed Brown failed to provide appropriate songwriter credits and compensation for the lyricist's contributions to the tracks.

cards.headline: Summer House Reunion Draws Record Audience
cards.teaser: The reality series achieved its highest viewership ever with the first two parts of its Season 10 reunion.
cards.body:
The Summer House Season 10 reunion delivered record ratings for the reality series. Part one drew the largest Live+Same Day audience in the show's history, according to NBCUniversal.

Both parts of the reunion marked a significant ratings milestone for the series, which follows a group sharing a summer house in the Hamptons.

cards.headline: Toy Story 5 Merchandise Expands Beyond Traditional Toys
cards.teaser: The upcoming film has inspired collaborations with brands including Away luggage and Pandora jewelry alongside expected toy releases.
cards.body:
Toy Story 5 has launched an expansive merchandise collection ahead of its theatrical release next weekend. Beyond traditional offerings like special-edition Uno cards, Funko Pops, and Lego sets, the franchise has partnered with unexpected brands including Away luggage and Pandora jewelry to create themed products.

The extensive merchandising effort reflects the film's themes. According to Tom Hanks, Toy Story 5 explores how toys compete with tablets for children's attention, addressing concerns about screen addiction among young viewers.

cards.headline: Adults Returns for Second Season in August
cards.teaser: FX announced the premiere date and guest stars for the comedy series starring Jake Shane and Gaten Matarazzo.
cards.body:
Adults will return for its second season on Aug. 27, with all eight episodes releasing simultaneously on FXX on-demand and Hulu at 9 p.m. ET. Two episodes will premiere weekly on FXX, and the series will be available on Disney+ internationally.

Guest stars for the season include Jake Shane and Gaten Matarazzo. The FX comedy series follows adult characters navigating relationships and personal challenges.

cards.headline: Craig Ferguson Says He Was Glad to Leave Late Night Before Trump Presidency
cards.teaser: The former Late Late Show host told a podcast he did not know how he would have handled covering the Trump era.
cards.body:
Craig Ferguson, the former host of CBS' The Late Late Show, recently expressed relief about stepping away from late-night television before Donald Trump's presidency. Speaking on Obsessed: The Podcast, Ferguson acknowledged uncertainty about how he would have managed covering a Trump administration while maintaining his show's comedic format.

His comments reflect the broader challenge faced by late-night hosts who remained on air during Trump's tenure, balancing political coverage with entertainment value.

cards.headline: Interpol Signs With Partisan Records, Announces Album
cards.teaser: The New York band will release their first album in four years through the Brooklyn indie label in August.
cards.body:
Interpol announced their first album in four years, This Mirror Weighs a Ton, arriving Aug. 28. The release marks the New York City band's first for Partisan Records, the Brooklyn-based independent label.

Andrew Wyatt produced the album, with David mixing the tracks. Partisan Records currently represents other artists including Geese. The label has established itself as a prominent independent in the music industry.

hero.headline: US launches strikes on Iran after helicopter downing
hero.body:
The United States military launched retaliatory strikes against Iran on Tuesday evening following Iran's downing of an American Apache helicopter near the Strait of Hormuz. US Central Command forces began the strikes at 5 p.m. Eastern Time at President Trump's direction, describing them as a proportional response.

The Apache helicopter crashed off the coast of Oman early Tuesday morning while on patrol. Both crew members were rescued in an unprecedented operation using an unmanned drone boat called a Corsair, a 24-foot vessel. The military confirmed both aviators were safe and uninjured after spending roughly two hours in the water.

President Trump announced the incident on Truth Social, stating that Iran had shot down the helicopter. "There were two pilots involved, both are safe and uninjured. Nevertheless, the United States must, of necessity, respond to the attack," Trump wrote. The actual cause of the crash remained under investigation, though Trump attributed it to Iranian action.

The retaliatory strikes came as tensions escalated in the Middle East following recent exchanges between Iran and Israel. Iranian state television reported that Israeli attacks killed at least two members of the country's air defense units. The region has remained unstable since the US and Israel began striking Iran on February 28, which has disrupted global energy prices and raised the cost of food and other essentials worldwide.

Apache helicopters have been critical assets for American military operations in the region, particularly for enforcing a blockade on Iranian crude oil shipments designed to pressure Tehran into making a deal. The helicopters have also been used by the United Arab Emirates to shoot down Iranian drones.

Despite the military action, Trump indicated he remains optimistic about negotiations with Iran. Earlier Tuesday, before the helicopter incident, Trump expressed confidence that a deal could be reached within "two or three days," though he provided no details supporting this assessment.

Trump previously stated that while the US could conduct extensive bombing campaigns, doing so would be costly in both lives and time. "If we go and bomb, which we could do very easily if we want, and we spend another two or three weeks bombing, they'll have nothing left whatsoever. But you won't have the strait open for months," he said. "If we do the bombing, you know, a lot of people are going to be killed. Who wants to do that? I don't."

Iranian state media reported explosions in Hormozgan province, which borders the Strait of Hormuz, following the announcement of US strikes. Central Command has not disclosed the specific targets of the military action.

The situation highlights the delicate balance the Trump administration is attempting to maintain: responding forcefully enough to the loss of military assets while preserving space for continued diplomatic negotiations with Iran.

cards.headline: House passes $70 billion immigration enforcement funding
cards.teaser: The reconciliation package funding ICE and Border Patrol passed 214-212 after weeks of delays.
cards.body:
The House passed a $70 billion budget reconciliation package on Tuesday to fund immigration enforcement agencies through the remainder of President Trump's term. The vote was 214-212, with Representative Kevin Kiley of California joining Democrats in opposition.

The legislation had stalled in the Senate for weeks before clearing the House. The funding will support the Department of Homeland Security, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and Border Patrol over the next three years as they carry out the administration's immigration enforcement priorities. President Trump is expected to sign the bill.

cards.headline: Trump faces pressure to drop intelligence nominee over spy powers renewal
cards.teaser: Democrats threaten to block FISA renewal unless the president withdraws Bill Pulte's nomination.
cards.body:
President Trump is set to meet with House Speaker Mike Johnson at the White House as pressure mounts to nominate a permanent director of national intelligence. The move comes as Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act faces a deadline for renewal by the end of the week.

Section 702 allows US intelligence agencies to collect communications of foreign targets overseas without a court warrant, though the surveillance can also capture communications involving Americans. Some Republicans believe appointing a permanent intelligence chief is necessary to save the controversial surveillance program before it expires.

cards.headline: Trump administration warns 500 hospitals over price transparency violations
cards.teaser: Warning letters went to hospitals failing to disclose costs of medical services as required.
cards.body:
The Trump administration has issued warning letters to more than 500 hospitals for failing to comply with federal price transparency requirements. These hospitals have not disclosed the costs of medical services to the public, as mandated by federal rules.

The administration contends that insufficient price transparency contributes to higher healthcare costs. Price transparency rules require hospitals to make pricing information publicly available, enabling consumers to compare costs across different facilities.

cards.headline: State Department launches premium visa interview service for $750
cards.teaser: The new program allows foreigners to secure visa appointments within 10 days for an additional fee.
cards.body:
The State Department will launch a premium expedited visa interview service next month for foreigners seeking US travel or business visas. Applicants can secure appointments within 10 days by paying an additional $750 fee, according to internal documents obtained by the Associated Press.

The program is expected to be announced in a Federal Register notice. The expedited service applies to visitor and business visa interviews, providing a faster track for those willing to pay the premium on top of standard visa application fees.

cards.headline: House reconciliation bill passes after stalling in Senate
cards.teaser: The $70 billion immigration enforcement package cleared the House 214-212.
cards.body:
The House passed a $70 billion budget reconciliation bill on Tuesday afternoon to fund immigration enforcement agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Border Patrol. The measure narrowly passed by a vote of 214-212 after stalling in the Senate for weeks.

The legislation now goes to President Trump's desk. The funding will support the administration's immigration enforcement priorities over the next three years, with Republicans backing the measure as Democrats raised concerns about congressional oversight.

cards.headline: US Central Command describes Iran strikes as proportional response
cards.teaser: The military action followed Iran shooting down an American Apache helicopter.
cards.body:
US Central Command launched strikes against Iran on Tuesday at 5 p.m. Eastern Time in response to Iran's downing of a US helicopter near the Strait of Hormuz on Monday. The military characterized the strikes as a proportional response carried out on orders from the Commander in Chief.

President Trump had indicated earlier Tuesday that the United States would respond to the helicopter incident. The latest exchange has raised concerns about potential military escalation between the two nations.
